clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive syndrome combining scalp and skin ichthyosis with neonatal sclerosing cholangitis, caused by mutations in CLDN1 encoding claudin-1
Cholestasis presents in the neonatal period with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a raised gamma-glutamyl transferase, unlike low-GGT inherited cholestases
Cholangiography demonstrates an irregular, beaded intrahepatic biliary tree typical of sclerosing cholangitis
Characteristic features include a scaly (ichthyotic) skin, scalp hypotrichosis or scarring alopecia, and sometimes oligodontia and dental anomalies
Claudin-1 is a tight-junction protein of biliary epithelium and skin; its loss disrupts the epithelial barrier in both organs
Diagnosis integrates the dermatological and cholestatic features with cholangiographic findings and CLDN1 sequencing
Management is supportive with ursodeoxycholic acid, fat-soluble vitamins, and skin care, with liver transplantation for progressive biliary cirrhosis
reference.pathophysiology: Neonatal ichthyosis-sclerosing cholangitis (NISCH) syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in CLDN1, which encodes claudin-1, an integral tight-junction protein maintaining paracellular barriers in the biliary epithelium and epidermis. Loss of claudin-1 disrupts these junctions, producing an ichthyotic skin phenotype and a sclerosing cholangitis in which bile leaks across a defective canalicular/ductular barrier and provokes biliary inflammation, strictures, and progressive fibrosis. The combination of high-GGT neonatal cholestasis with ichthyosis and scalp involvement is characteristic.
additionalDifferentials: Primary sclerosing cholangitis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests and gamma-glutamyl transferase (characteristically raised)
Serum bile acids and fractionated bilirubin
Cholangiography (MRCP or intraoperative) showing irregular sclerosing bile ducts
Liver biopsy demonstrating ductular reaction, cholangitis, and fibrosis
Dermatological assessment and skin examination for ichthyosis and hypotrichosis
redFlags: Progressive biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension
Vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy in the cholestatic neonate
Recurrent cholangitis with fever and worsening jaundice
Failure to thrive from fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
reference.prognosis: The sclerosing cholangitis is usually progressive, and many children develop biliary cirrhosis requiring liver transplantation over time; the cutaneous features persist but are managed supportively, and outcome depends chiefly on the hepatic course.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnostic significance of coexisting ichthyosis and scalp involvement in a cholestatic infant
Confusing the cholangiographic appearance with biliary atresia
Assuming a low GGT, which does not fit and can delay the correct diagnosis
Neglecting fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and skin care
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Suchy, Sokol & Balistreri, Liver Disease in Children
management: Manage the cholestasis with ursodeoxycholic acid and choleretic support to improve bile flow
Supplement fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) and provide medium-chain-triglyceride-enriched nutrition to counter fat malabsorption and support growth
Control cholestatic pruritus with agents such as rifampicin or a bile-acid sequestrant
Treat the ichthyosis supportively with emollients and keratolytic skin care under dermatology
Monitor liver function and disease progression, surveying for biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension
Refer for liver transplantation as the sclerosing cholangitis progresses to end-stage liver disease
Confirm the diagnosis with CLDN1 sequencing and provide genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive condition
